quiz_epi:1.q: A pathology report describes a tumor arising from the secretory cells of a gland. Under the lecture's four basic tissue types, to which tissue do these cells belong?
quiz_epi:1.r: The four basic tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous, and glandular secretion is listed as a main function of epithelial tissue (p. 129). The faculty question on p. 184 makes the same point: glandular is not a basic tissue type.

quiz_epi:10.q: Which statement about the cells of this epithelium is correct?
o: All cells reach the free surface
Surface cells are dead and keratinized
All cells touch the basal lamina
quiz_epi:10.r: This is pseudostratified epithelium of the trachea (p. 141). Nuclei sit at different levels so it looks layered, but it is a single layer: all cells touch the basal lamina, and some may not reach the surface (p. 207).
quiz_epi:10.alt: Light micrograph of a tall epithelium with nuclei at several levels, a fringe along the free surface, and several pale granular cells.

quiz_epi:11.q: This epithelium lines a hollow organ. For which function is it specialised?
quiz_epi:11.r: Several layers topped by dome shaped surface cells is transitional epithelium (p. 142), a unique epithelium suited to stretching whose number of layers varies with distension of the organ (p. 207). It lines the urinary system from renal calyces to urethra (p. 143).
quiz_epi:11.alt: Light micrograph of a multilayered epithelium with large rounded cells at the free surface, resting on pink connective tissue.

quiz_epi:12.q: Tracer molecules placed in the lumen stop at the structure marked by the arrow. Which transmembrane proteins form this structure?
quiz_epi:12.r: The junction that stops movement between the lumen and the intercellular space is the zonula occludens, or tight junction (p. 145). Its seal comes from the transmembrane proteins claudin and occludin of each cell (p. 146).
quiz_epi:12.alt: Drawing of three epithelial cells below a lumen filled with yellow tracer dots; a yellow arrow points to a spot high on the border between two cells.

quiz_epi:13.q: This electron micrograph shows the apical junctions between two intestinal epithelial cells. The arrow marks the junction lying immediately below the tight junction. Which of the following alters the function of this junction?
quiz_epi:13.r: The zonula adherens encircles the cell immediately below the zonula occludens (p. 149). Bacteroides fragilis enterotoxin alters zonula adherens function and is associated with acute diarrheal disease (p. 151). Zonulin acts on the tight junction (p. 147).
quiz_epi:13.alt: Electron micrograph of the border between two cells running down from the surface, with a yellow arrow pointing at one level of the border.

quiz_epi:14.q: In this drawing of a spot-like cell junction, the green transmembrane proteins insert into a red cytoplasmic plaque that binds the blue filaments. Which pairing identifies the green proteins and the blue filaments?
quiz_epi:14.r: A desmosome has transmembrane desmoglein and desmocollin (cadherin family) inserting into a plaque of plakoglobin and desmoplakin, which binds keratin (p. 154). Cadherins with actin is the zonula adherens (p. 149); integrins with keratin is the hemidesmosome (p. 155, p. 205).
quiz_epi:14.alt: Drawing of two cell membranes joined by green proteins, with a red plaque on each side and blue filaments looping onto each plaque.

quiz_epi:15.q: A 24-year-old athlete has life-threatening arrhythmias. At transplantation the right ventricle is massively enlarged with near absence of lateral wall myocytes. Genes encoding the proteins of which structure are mutated?
quiz_epi:15.r: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia is caused by mutations in genes encoding desmosomal proteins (p. 156). The gap junction disease on the slides is Charcot-Marie-Tooth X, from a connexin-32 mutation (p. 160).

quiz_epi:16.q: The arrows mark attachment sites along the basal surface of epithelial cells. Which transmembrane proteins anchor the cells at these sites?
quiz_epi:16.r: These are hemidesmosomes, the faculty answer on p. 188. In hemidesmosomes cadherins are replaced with integrins to anchor the cell to the basal lamina (p. 155).
quiz_epi:16.alt: Two electron micrographs labelled a and b, each with black arrows pointing at small dense spots along the lower border of cells.

quiz_epi:18.q: The drawing and freeze-fracture replica show one type of cell junction. What does this junction allow?
quiz_epi:18.r: Gap junctions mediate rapid communication: small molecules such as sodium, potassium and chloride pass through channels less than 1.5 nm in size for coordinated function such as rhythmic contractions (p. 158). Each channel is two aligned connexons of six connexins (p. 159).
quiz_epi:18.alt: Left: drawing of two membranes crossed by a cluster of small paired channels. Right: grayscale replica showing a patch of closely packed particles.

quiz_epi:19.q: In a salivary gland, the capsule and septa form the connective tissue that supports the secretory cells. What is this supporting tissue called?
quiz_epi:19.r: The secretory cells of a gland are the parenchyma, and the connective tissue within the gland that supports them is the stroma (p. 161). The exocrine gland drawing labels the septum and capsule as stroma (p. 166).

quiz_epi:2.q: Which technique was used to produce the brown staining of the cells in this image?
quiz_epi:2.r: This is the faculty practice image: peroxidase staining of proteins in epithelial cells (p. 185). An antibody linked to an enzyme such as horseradish peroxidase gives a colored precipitate with its substrate (p. 194).
quiz_epi:2.alt: Light micrograph of glandular tissue in which many cells are stained brown against a pale blue background.

quiz_epi:20.q: The arrows mark pale, granular cells scattered among the other cells of this epithelium. How are these cells classified as glands?
quiz_epi:20.r: Goblet cells are the handout's example of a unicellular gland (p. 210), and they are listed among the exocrine glands as mucous cells (p. 211). The image is on p. 104.
quiz_epi:20.alt: Light micrograph of a tall epithelium with four black arrows pointing at pale, granular, swollen cells among darker neighbours.

quiz_epi:21.q: Two arrangements of secretory cells in ductless glands are shown. Which organ is the lecture's example of arrangement A?
quiz_epi:21.r: Endocrine cells are arranged either in cords, as in pancreatic islets, or in follicles (hollow balls in which secretory product is stored), as in the thyroid (p. 210). Arrangement A is the follicle (p. 164).
quiz_epi:21.alt: Two line drawings of secretory cells wrapped by a capillary: in A the cells surround a central space, in B the cells fill the whole cluster.

quiz_epi:22.q: What is the classification of this gland?
quiz_epi:22.r: This is the faculty practice image and the answer on the slide is simple tubular (p. 187): one straight unbranched tube whose whole length is secretory. The handout's example is the crypts of Lieberkuhn (p. 212).
quiz_epi:22.alt: Light micrograph of straight, test-tube shaped glands lying side by side and opening onto a surface at the top.

quiz_epi:24.q: Three modes of secretion are drawn. Which gland releases its product by the mode shown in C?
quiz_epi:24.r: C shows the whole cell being shed, which is holocrine secretion (p. 170): the product is extruded along with the entire cell contents, as in the sebaceous gland (p. 211). A is merocrine (parotid, pancreas) and B is apocrine (mammary gland).
quiz_epi:24.alt: Three line drawings of secretory cells labelled A, B and C, each with an upward arrow showing how product leaves the cell.

quiz_epi:26.q: The black arrows mark the apical border of these intestinal cells as seen by light microscopy. What makes up this border?
quiz_epi:26.r: The slide shows simple columnar epithelium of small intestine with a microvillous brush border at the black arrows (p. 172). Microvilli plus glycocalyx equals the brush border, as seen in the light microscope (p. 206).
quiz_epi:26.alt: Light micrograph of tall columnar cells with a thin dense line along the free surface marked by two black arrows; two white arrows mark small dark cells lower down.

quiz_epi:27.q: In this electron micrograph of the apical surface of an intestinal cell, what is the function of the filament layer at the yellow arrow?
o: Holds a layer of protective mucin
Binds the cell to basal lamina
quiz_epi:27.r: The layer is the terminal web (p. 174), an actin-dense region in the apical cytoplasm where microvilli are anchored (p. 204). Its actin filaments help anchor the actin filaments that originate from the microvilli (p. 149).
quiz_epi:27.alt: Electron micrograph of short finger-like projections with a fuzzy coat above them; a yellow arrow points to a band of filaments in the cytoplasm just below their bases.

quiz_epi:28.q: The yellow arrow marks the structure into which one of these apical projections is anchored. How are its microtubules arranged?
o: Nine triplets and no central pair
Nine doublets and no central pair
quiz_epi:28.r: Cilia are anchored into basal bodies, which are microtubules in a nine triplet arrangement analogous to centrioles, seen as electron dense structures at the apical pole (p. 206). Nine doublets around two singlets is the shaft of the cilium, shown in the inset (p. 180).
quiz_epi:28.alt: Electron micrograph of long apical projections cut lengthwise, with an inset of the projections in cross-section; a yellow arrow points to a dense structure at the base of one projection.

quiz_epi:29.q: This epithelium lines the ductus epididymis. What is the function of its long apical projections?
quiz_epi:29.r: These are stereocilia (p. 181). The name is a misnomer: they are not cilia and not motile; they are elongated microvilli that increase surface area and facilitate absorption, as in the epididymis and ductus deferens (p. 206).
quiz_epi:29.alt: Light micrograph of a tall epithelium with very long, fine, wispy projections extending from the cell surface into the lumen.

quiz_epi:6.q: A biopsy of thick stratified squamous epithelium contains no blood vessels within the epithelium itself. How do its cells obtain nutrients?
quiz_epi:6.r: Epithelial tissue is avascular and is nourished by diffusion from vasculature in the underlying connective tissue (p. 130), which the handout calls the lamina propria (p. 204).

quiz_epi:7.q: The arrowheads mark nuclei of the cells that line this structure. For which functions is this type of epithelium suited?
quiz_epi:7.r: The lining is endothelium, a simple squamous epithelium: flat cells whose nuclei are plumper than the rest of the cell. These cells are suited to diffusion and filtration (p. 133, p. 207).
quiz_epi:7.alt: Light micrograph of a round thin-walled structure cut in cross-section, with three white arrowheads on flattened nuclei of its lining.

quiz_epi:8.q: According to the lecture, where is this type of epithelium found?
quiz_epi:8.r: Two layers of cuboidal cells is stratified cuboidal epithelium, the faculty answer on p. 186. It is rare and lines the ducts of sweat glands (p. 143, p. 209).
quiz_epi:8.alt: Light micrograph of a round lumen surrounded by an epithelium with round nuclei at two levels.

quiz_epi:9.q: Which statement describes the cells in the layer at the yellow arrow?
quiz_epi:9.r: This is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of thick skin (p. 138). Its surface layer is dead: the cells lose all organelles, including the nucleus, and become a bundle of keratin (p. 209). The dividing cells are the deep basal cells.
quiz_epi:9.alt: Light micrograph of a thick multilayered epithelium; a yellow arrow points into the wide pale layer at the surface.

quiz_epi_b:1.q: This micrograph gives a three-dimensional surface view of fractured kidney tubules. What is the highest magnification the lecture gives for the microscope that produced it?
quiz_epi_b:1.r: A 3-D surface view is scanning electron microscopy (p. 96), and the SEM slide gives magnification up to 100,000 times (p. 93). The light microscope reaches 1,500 times (p. 91) and the TEM 500,000 times (p. 92).
quiz_epi_b:1.alt: Grey-scale micrograph of broken-open tubules seen in relief, with a letter P on one tubule

quiz_epi_b:2.q: In this course the basement membrane is the layer beneath an epithelium that one stain reveals by light microscopy. According to the lecture's stain list, what else does that stain demonstrate?
quiz_epi_b:2.r: The basement membrane is defined as a PAS-positive layer seen by light microscopy (p. 130), and Periodic Acid Schiff stains glycogen and glycoproteins (p. 103). Hematoxylin stains nuclei, aldehyde fuchsin and orcein stain elastic fibers, and silver stains the Golgi apparatus and reticular fibers.

quiz_epi_b:3.q: A tissue sample shows several types of fixed and wandering cells separated by abundant extracellular matrix. According to the lecture's table of the four basic tissues, what is the main function of this tissue?
quiz_epi_b:3.r: Fixed and wandering cells in abundant matrix is connective tissue, whose main functions are support and protection (p. 129). Epithelium has a small amount of matrix, muscle a moderate amount, and nervous tissue none.

quiz_epi_b:4.q: The surface cells of this two-layered epithelium are taller than they are wide. According to the lecture, in which structure is this type of epithelium found?
quiz_epi_b:4.r: Two layers with columnar surface cells is stratified columnar epithelium, shown in a salivary gland duct (p. 140; large excretory ducts of glands, p. 143). Sweat gland ducts are stratified cuboidal (p. 139) and kidney collecting ducts and thyroid follicles are simple cuboidal (p. 134).
quiz_epi_b:4.alt: Orange-stained micrograph of a curved epithelial wall around a lumen, with two black arrows marking its outer and inner borders

quiz_epi_b:5.q: Two kinds of gland form from covering epithelium by the routes drawn. How do the glands labelled B deliver their secretory product?
o: Onto the surface of the body
Into the cavity of a hollow organ
quiz_epi_b:5.r: In route B the duct cells disappear, so the gland loses its connection to the surface: an endocrine gland (p. 163), whose product passes directly into the blood stream (p. 164). Exocrine glands (A) keep ducts that carry the product to the body surface or into a hollow organ (p. 165).
quiz_epi_b:5.alt: Drawing of surface epithelium growing down into connective tissue along two routes, ending in a gland labelled A on the left and two glands labelled B on the right

quiz_epi_b:6.q: This drawing comes from the lecture's classification of exocrine glands; the duct is yellow and the secretory portion is red. How is this gland classified?
quiz_epi_b:6.r: One unbranched duct makes the gland simple (p. 167), and several rounded secretory sacs opening into that one duct make it branched acinar (p. 168). In a compound gland the duct itself branches.
quiz_epi_b:6.alt: Drawing of a single gland with a yellow-lined stalk at the top and red-lined portions below

quiz_epi_b:7.q: Three modes of secretion are drawn. Which option names the modes in drawings A and B, in that order?
quiz_epi_b:7.r: On the Mode of Secretion slide (p. 170), the cell releasing small vesicles at its apex is merocrine, the cell losing its apical portion is apocrine, and the cell shed whole is holocrine.
quiz_epi_b:7.alt: Line drawings of three secretory cells labelled A, B and C, each releasing its product in a different way

quiz_epi_b:8.q: A boy has weak foot and lower leg muscles and high arches caused by an X-linked point mutation. The mutated protein is a subunit of the channels in this drawing; which protein is it?
quiz_epi_b:8.r: The drawing is a gap junction: six connexin proteins form a connexon, and two aligned connexons form an open channel (p. 159). Charcot-Marie-Tooth X disease is caused by a point mutation in the connexin-32 gene on the X chromosome (p. 160).
quiz_epi_b:8.alt: Drawing of two stacked red membrane sheets crossed by green cylinders, each cylinder made of a ring of subunits around a central pore

brief:
Techniques, Epithelium and Glands High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Techniques, Epithelium and Glands (Djakiew) was 29/46 (63%) on your September quiz, with surface specializations weakest at 2/7. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 88 to 189, handout pp. 190 to 213. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides). The "how to recognise it" columns are my descriptions of his own images.

1. The three microscopes (LO 1)

The three instruments differ in what carries the image (light, transmitted electrons, or secondary electrons), and that sets the magnification and resolution.

Feature Light microscope (LM) Transmission electron microscope (TEM) Scanning electron microscope (SEM) Page
How it focuses Glass lenses focus light Magnets focus a beam of electrons Electromagnetic lenses plus a scan generator 91, 92, 197
What forms the image Transmitted light Transmitted primary electrons on a fluorescent screen Secondary electrons collected by a signal detector, shown on a cathode ray tube 195, 197, 199
Magnification Up to 1,500 Up to 500,000 Up to 100,000 91, 92, 93
Resolution 0.2 micron 1 to 1.5 nm 2 to 10 nm 194, 196, 197
Picture 2 dimensional, in colour 2 dimensional, black and white 3 dimensional surface 199
Same kidney tubule Pink cells, fuzzy lumen edge Individual microvilli and organelles Carpeted inner surface of a broken tubule 94, 95, 96
Shared by both electron microscopes Page
Vacuum pump, so electrons can flow 195, 197
Electron source is a tungsten filament 195, 197
Unit Size Use Page
Micrometer 10^-6 m; a red cell is 7 to 9 Light microscope 190
Nanometer (nm) 10^-9 m; plasma membrane is 7.5 to 10 Electron microscope 190
Angstrom 10^-10 m Older electron microscope unit 190

Resolution is the minimum distance at which two close structures can still be told apart, and a higher numerical aperture gives better resolution (p. 194).

Type of light microscopy What it is Page
Brightfield Light shines through a stained specimen; the most common 194
Fluorescence Ultraviolet light excites the specimen to emit visible light 194
Phase contrast Good for living and unstained specimens, such as cultured cells 194

One small conflict: the slide says SEM magnifies "up to 100,000 times" (p. 93) and the handout says "in excess of 100,000" (p. 197). Answer 100,000 either way.

2. Preparing tissue, and the stains (LO 2)

Every method fixes and dehydrates; they differ in what supports the tissue and what gives contrast.

Step LM TEM SEM Page
Fixation Formalin (cross-links proteins) Glutaraldehyde (proteins, nucleic acids), then osmium tetroxide (lipids) Same as TEM 191, 195, 197
Dehydration Ethanol (alcohol or acetone) Ethanol Ethanol 97, 109, 124
Support Paraffin embedding Plastic (Epon), then polymerized None; critical point drying avoids drying artifacts 98, 110, 197
Sectioning Microtome, steel knife, 2 to 10 micrometers Ultramicrotome, glass or diamond knife, 20 to 100 nm None 191, 195
Mounting Glass slide Wire mesh grid Glued to a metal stub 191, 195, 197
Contrast Coloured stains Heavy metals: uranyl acetate, lead citrate Gold or palladium coat, to enhance electron emission 195, 197
Preparation time 4 to 5 days 2 to 3 days 5 to 8 hours 199

Three conflicts to know. (1) Fixative: the slides list formalin for TEM and SEM as well (pp. 109, 124), while the handout says glutaraldehyde then osmium tetroxide (p. 195) and "same as TEM" for SEM (p. 197). Answer his handout wording unless a question quotes the slide. (2) TEM section thickness: the handout text says 20 to 100 nm (p. 195) but its Table 1 says 100 to 600 angstroms, which is 10 to 60 nm (p. 199). Use 20 to 100 nm. (3) Xylene: the slide puts it under dehydration (p. 97), the handout's Figure 4 calls it clearing (p. 192).

Stain What it shows Page
Hematoxylin Blue, positively charged dye; stains negatively charged structures such as DNA (the nucleus). These are "basophilic" 103, 193
Eosin Pink-orange, negatively charged dye; stains positively charged substances such as hemoglobin (the cytoplasm). These are "eosinophilic" 103, 193
Periodic acid Schiff (PAS) Glycogen, glycoproteins; red product. The basement membrane is PAS-positive 103, 130, 193
Aldehyde fuchsin Elastic fibers; also B-cells of pancreatic islets 103, 193
Orcein Elastic fibers, dark brown (slide adds collagen fibers and cytoplasmic counterstain) 103, 193
Silver Reticular fibers (type III collagen), black (slide adds Golgi apparatus) 103, 193
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) fact Detail Page
Principle Antibodies show where a specific antigen protein is 106
Direct The primary antibody carries the label 194
Indirect A labeled second antibody binds the first; amplifies the signal 106, 194
Labels for LM Fluorescent compound (fluorescein, rhodamine) or enzyme (horseradish peroxidase, gives a colored precipitate) 194
Label for TEM Gold particles of different sizes 195
Frozen sections (cryostat) Preserve antigenicity; morphology is not as good as paraffin 193
How to recognise it Brown cells on a pale blue background 107, 185

3. Freeze fracture: P-face versus E-face (LO 2)

Freeze fracture splits a membrane down the middle of its bilayer, so you look at the inside of each half, never at the true surface (p. 196).

Step Detail Page
1 Physical fixation by rapid freezing (liquid nitrogen or freon); no chemical fixative 199
2 Fracture under high vacuum; the plane follows the hydrophobic middle of the membrane 196, 199
3 Coat with platinum and carbon to make a metal replica 199
4 Digest the cells away; view the replica in the TEM 196, 199
Face Which half of the bilayer Particles On his slide Page
P-face Inner half, the half next to the cytoplasm Most of the integral protein particles The heavily studded side 123, 196
E-face Outer half, the half next to the outside of the cell Few particles; smoother The finer, emptier side 123, 196

The handout sentence that confused you: "the E-face, the inwardly facing outer half, and the P-face, the outwardly facing inner half" (p. 196). Read it in two parts. "Outer half" and "inner half" say which leaflet you have. "Inwardly facing" and "outwardly facing" only say which way the newly exposed surface points: the outer leaflet's fractured surface looks in toward the cell, and the inner leaflet's fractured surface looks out. So: P-face = inner half = many particles. E-face = outer half = few particles. Memory aid, P for protoplasm and E for extracellular (outside the slides).

4. Four basic tissues, and what makes an epithelium (LO 3)

There are four basic tissues, and glandular is not one of them: glands are epithelium (pp. 129, 184).

Tissue Cells Extracellular matrix Main function (p. 129)
Epithelial Aggregated polyhedral cells Small amount Lining of surfaces or body cavities; glandular secretion
Connective Several types of fixed and wandering cells Abundant Support and protection
Muscle Elongated contractile cells Moderate Movement
Nervous Intertwining elongated processes None Transmission of nervous impulses
Feature of every epithelium Detail Page
Where Covers or lines all body surfaces except joint cavities 130
Avascular Nourished by diffusion from vessels in the underlying connective tissue (lamina propria); diffusion is rate limiting 130, 204
Basal lamina Every epithelium sits on one 130
Polarity Apical, lateral and basal sides; the zonula occludens marks the border between apical and basolateral 130, 206
Strength Keratin filaments plus desmosomes make it act like one sheet 130
Renewal Intestine 2 to 3 days; epidermis 28 days; from stem cells 204
Metaplasia Reversible change from one epithelial type to another 207
Mesothelium Epithelium lining the pleural, pericardial and peritoneal cavities 130
Endothelium Epithelium lining the cardiovascular channels 130
Germ layer Epithelia it gives Page
Ectoderm Skin, sweat glands, oral cavity, vagina, anus 203
Mesoderm Endothelium, mesothelium, genital and urinary systems 203
Endoderm Esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, liver, pancreas, respiratory system 203
Basolateral surface job Page
Receives chemical messengers such as hormones 206
Sodium-potassium pump; seen as an infolded basal membrane with many mitochondria 206
ATP-dependent nutrient uptake 206

5. Classifying epithelium (LO 4)

Name an epithelium by the number of layers and then by the shape of the surface cells only (pp. 131, 207).

Word Meaning Page
Simple One layer; all cells touch the basal lamina 207
Stratified Several layers; not all cells touch the basal lamina 207
Pseudostratified Looks layered because nuclei sit at different levels, but all cells touch the basal lamina; some do not reach the surface 207
Squamous Flat, scale-like; the nucleus bulges 133, 207
Cuboidal As wide as tall; round central nucleus 134, 207
Columnar Taller than wide; oval nucleus, central or basal 207
Type How to recognise it in an image Function Where Page
Simple squamous One thin line of flat cells; only the plump nuclei show Diffusion and filtration Endothelium, mesothelium, Bowman's capsule, thin loop of Henle, alveoli, rete testis 133, 143
Simple cuboidal One row of square cells with round central nuclei around a lumen Lining ducts; secretion, absorption Thyroid follicles, kidney distal tubules and collecting ducts, choroid plexus, gland ducts, ovary surface 134, 143
Simple columnar One row of tall cells; oval nuclei lined up Secretion and absorption Stomach, small and large intestine, gallbladder, uterus, oviducts, small bronchi 135, 143
Pseudostratified columnar Tall cells, nuclei at several levels; often cilia and goblet cells Trachea, bronchi, epididymis, Eustachian tube 141, 143
Stratified squamous, nonkeratinized Many layers; flat surface cells still have nuclei Covers wet surfaces; surface layer is alive Mouth, esophagus, vagina 137, 209
Stratified squamous, keratinized Many layers under a thick pale layer with no nuclei Tough; resists wear and tear. Surface cells are dead bundles of keratin Skin 138, 209
Stratified cuboidal Two rings of round nuclei around a duct lumen Rare; usually two layers Sweat gland ducts 139, 186, 209
Stratified columnar Tall surface cells on cuboidal or polyhedral deep cells Rare Salivary gland duct, cavernous urethra, conjunctiva 140, 143, 209
Transitional Several layers; dome shaped surface cells, some binucleate Stretching; layer number changes with distension Renal calyces to urethra (ureter, bladder) 142, 143, 207

Transitional epithelium is layered but is not called "stratified" (p. 209). The handout calls stratified squamous a "tough endothelium" (p. 209); that is a typing slip for epithelium.

6. Cell junctions (LO 8)

From the apex down the order is tight junction, zonula adherens, desmosome, with gap junctions lower and hemidesmosomes on the basal surface (pp. 144, 153).

Junction Other name Shape and place Transmembrane proteins Filaments Job Page
Zonula occludens Tight junction Band around the apical end Claudin, occludin Barrier: stops molecules passing between cells; keeps polarity 145, 146
Zonula adherens Intermediate junction, adhesion belt Band just below the tight junction Cadherins (bind catenin) Actin Anchors cells to each other; its actin forms the terminal web 149
Desmosome Macula adherens "Spot welds" around the cell Desmoglein, desmocollin (cadherin family); plaque of plakoglobin and desmoplakin Keratin Attaches cells to each other 153, 154
Hemidesmosome Half-desmosome Basal surface Integrins (replace cadherins) Keratin Anchors the cell to the basal lamina; in high-stress tissue such as skin 153, 155, 205
Gap junction Communicating junction Patches on lateral membrane Six connexins make a connexon; two connexons make a channel Small molecules (sodium, potassium, chloride) pass through channels under 1.5 nm; rapid signalling, rhythmic contraction 158, 159
Junction How to recognise it in an image Page
Zonula occludens Most apical; the two membranes touch; tracer from the lumen stops there 145, 150
Zonula adherens Just below it; membranes run parallel with a fuzzy actin mat 149, 150
Desmosome Lower; a dark disc with filaments streaming into a dense plaque on both sides 150, 154
Hemidesmosome Small dark half-plaques along the basal membrane facing the basal lamina 155, 188
Gap junction Freeze fracture shows a round patch of packed particles; in section, two membranes very close and parallel 158
Disease or toxin Junction hit Detail Page
Zonulin Zonula occludens Toxin secreted by Vibrio cholerae; changes tight junction permeability in the gut; implicated in celiac disease 147
Bacteroides fragilis enterotoxin Zonula adherens Acute diarrheal disease 151
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia Desmosome Mutations in genes for desmosomal proteins; arrhythmias, enlarged right ventricle 156
Charcot-Marie-Tooth X disease Gap junction Point mutation in connexin-32 on the X chromosome; Schwann cells; weak foot and lower leg, high arches 160

Terminal bars are the tight junction and zonula adherens seen as dots in the light microscope (p. 204). Neurons have desmosome-like structures called synaptic clefts (p. 153).

7. Basal lamina and basement membrane (LO 4)

The basal lamina is an electron microscope structure; the basement membrane is the thicker PAS-positive line seen with the light microscope (pp. 130, 204).

Term Seen with Made of Page
Basal lamina TEM only Type IV collagen, laminin, entactin, heparan sulfate proteoglycan; secreted by the epithelial cell 130, 204
Lamina densa TEM Electron dense layer, 20 to 100 nm thick 204
Lamina lucida TEM Electron lucent layer on one or both sides of the densa 204
Reticular lamina Type III collagen; secreted by connective tissue cells 204
Basement membrane LM, PAS-positive Usually basal lamina plus reticular lamina; two fused basal laminae in glomerulus and alveoli 204
Attachment Chain Page
Ordinary cell to basal lamina Actin, integrin, laminin, type IV collagen 205
Hemidesmosome to basal lamina Cytokeratin, integrin, laminin, type IV collagen 205
Basal lamina to reticular lamina Anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen 205
Function of the basal lamina Page
Structural support 205
Filter for molecules and cells 205
Needed for cell polarity 205
Binds growth factors 205
Pathway for cell migration, as in wound healing 205

The collagen numbers in one line: IV is in the basal lamina, III is in the reticular lamina, VII ties the two together.

8. Surface specializations (LO 8)

Microvilli and stereocilia have actin and do not move; cilia have microtubules and do move (p. 206).

Structure Core Size Motile Function Where Page
Microvilli Actin filaments, tied by fimbrin and villin 1 micrometer high More surface area for absorption Small intestine, proximal renal tubule 176, 206
Stereocilia Elongated, thin microvilli; "not cilia" No More surface area; facilitate absorption. Sensory in the organ of Corti Epididymis, ductus deferens 181, 206
Cilia Microtubules, 9 doublets around 2 singlets; dynein arms with ATPase 5 to 10 micrometers high Yes Move fluid and particles Trachea, bronchi, oviduct 206
Flagellum Essentially a long cilium One per cell; only on spermatozoa 207
Microplicae Small ridge-like elevations of membrane May help hold a layer of protective mucin "Wet" epithelia: oral cavity, esophagus 207
Structure How to recognise it in an image Page
Microvilli LM: a thin dense line on the cell tops. TEM: short even fingers with a fuzzy coat. SEM: a short dense carpet 172, 173, 174
Stereocilia LM: very long, fine, wispy strands reaching far into the lumen. SEM: tangled threads 181, 182
Cilia LM: a hair-like fringe above a dark line of basal bodies. TEM cross-section: a ring of nine doublets with two in the centre 141, 180
